fable-5.1.text:
Well, first I want to be clear. I think the technology is going to be enormously impactful. It's going to raise productivity in a way that's probably as big as, maybe bigger than, anything we've seen in our lifetimes. So the problem isn't the technology. The problem is the difference between how great the technology is and what you're paying for it, and how you're paying for it.

If you look at history, every great new technology produced the same dynamic. The canals, the railroads, radio in the 1920s, the internet in 1999. The technology changed the world, and a lot of the companies that built it went broke, and the people who invested in them lost most of their money. That's because the amount of money that went in was much greater than what could be earned back in the time it had to be earned back.

The way it works is pretty mechanical. Prices go up, and people buy because prices are going up. They extrapolate, and the extrapolation gets built into the price. Then they borrow to buy, new buyers come in who were never in before, and it becomes a very large percentage of the stock market and of everybody's portfolio. We're at that stage now. A handful of companies are a huge share of the market, and they're spending enormous amounts on chips and data centers and power, and more and more of that spending is being financed with debt. So you have a lot of capital that has to be paid back, and it has to be paid back with earnings that haven't arrived yet.

What pops it is usually not that the technology disappoints. It's that money gets tight. Interest rates go up, or liquidity goes away, or the earnings come in a bit slower than the price assumed, and the people who are leveraged have to sell. And because it's such a large part of the economy and the markets, when that happens it doesn't just hurt the people who bought the stocks. It hurts everybody.

Then there's a second problem, which honestly I worry about more. The productivity gains go to the people who own the technology and the people who have the skills to use it. The people being replaced by it don't get them. So you get a bigger wealth gap and a bigger values gap, and when you have those in a democracy, you get internal conflict. And on top of that, this is the center of the competition between the United States and China, so it's a geopolitical fight too. So you have a bubble dynamic, a wealth gap dynamic, and a great power conflict dynamic all wrapped up in the same thing. That's why I say it creates problems.

r001.rationale: The response describes enormous AI infrastructure spending and says future earnings have not arrived, but it does not explain that competition pressures developers to make those investments.

opus-5.5.text:
Well, I don't think AI itself is the problem. I think it's probably the most powerful technology any of us will see in our lifetimes, and it's going to raise productivity enormously. The problem is the dynamic around it, and I've seen this pattern many times over the 50-plus years I've been doing this.

When there's a great new technology, people get excited, and that excitement turns into money pouring in. The prices of those companies go up, which attracts more buyers, which pushes prices up further. At some point the prices reflect much more than any realistic future earnings could justify. That's the classic bubble dynamic. It happened with railroads, with radio and the automobile in the 1920s, and with the internet in the late '90s. In each case the technology was real and changed the world, and many investors still lost a great deal of money. You can be right about the technology and wrong about the investment.

Now look at what's happening. A huge share of the stock market's gains, and of economic growth itself, is coming from a handful of companies spending enormous sums on chips, data centers and electricity. Increasingly that spending is being financed with debt. So you have concentration: a lot of people's wealth, pensions and expectations are riding on the same bet. Bubbles don't usually pop just because people realize prices are too high. They pop when somebody needs cash. Debts come due, interest rates go up, there's a tax on wealth, or something forces people to sell assets to raise money. Then everybody heads for the door at the same time.

The second problem is what it does to the wealth gap. AI is going to benefit the people who own the technology and the people who know how to use it, which is roughly the top 10 or 20 percent. A lot of people in the middle are going to find their jobs displaced or their wages pressured. We already have the largest wealth and values gaps we've had since the 1930s, and you can see the populism of the left and the right growing out of that. If AI makes that gap wider, that's a social and political problem, not just an economic one.

The third piece is geopolitical. This is a technology war between the United States and China. Whoever wins it will likely win the economic and military competition. So countries won't slow down, even where slowing down might be prudent, and that adds risk.

When I put those together, a debt-financed investment boom concentrated in a few places, widening inequality, and great-power conflict, they look a lot like the conditions I've studied in prior big cycles. My principle is: don't fight the technology, but don't confuse a great technology with a great investment at any price. Diversify well, understand what's being financed with debt, and watch for what will force people to sell.

fable-5.text:
Well, let me explain the dynamic, because it's a classic one that we've seen repeated through history. When you have a new, transformative technology — and AI is certainly that — enormous amounts of money pour into it. And that money has to come from somewhere. Right now, we're seeing hundreds of billions of dollars going into chips, data centers, infrastructure, and a lot of it is being financed with debt or with equity prices that assume spectacular future earnings.

Now here's the problem. The technology being great and the investment being profitable are two different things. If you go back to 1998, 1999, the internet was real — it changed everything, just like people said it would. But most of the companies that were invested in didn't produce the returns to justify their prices, and we had a bubble that burst. So you can be right about the technology and still lose a lot of money. The question you always have to ask is: how much are you paying, and will the earnings come through to justify that? When I look at the amounts being spent today relative to the revenues actually coming in, there's a big gap that has to be filled by future profits that are uncertain.

And then there's the second dynamic, which is who benefits. AI is going to be a fantastic productivity tool, but productivity gains don't flow evenly. It will make some people and some companies enormously wealthy while displacing others, and that widens the wealth gap at a time when we already have large wealth and values gaps and a lot of political conflict. History shows that when you have a big wealth gap combined with economic stress, you get populism of the left and populism of the right, and you get fighting over how the pie is divided rather than growing it.

So you have these two things happening at once: a financial dynamic, where the investment boom is supporting the economy but creating bubble risks and more debt, and a social dynamic, where the benefits are concentrated. If the returns disappoint, the correction hits an economy that's already stretched. That's why I say it's a two-edged sword — it's not that AI is bad, it's that the way it's being financed and the way its gains are distributed create problems we need to be honest about.

opus-5.text:
Well, let me take you through the mechanics of it, because I don't look at AI as good or bad — I look at it as a force that has consequences, and some of those consequences are wonderful and some of them are problems.

The first thing is, it's being financed. Enormous amounts of capital are going into building this out — the chips, the data centers, the power. And when you have a new technology that everybody agrees is going to change the world, what happens is that the agreement gets priced in and then some. I've studied bubbles going back to the 1920s, the Nifty Fifty, the dot-com period, and there's a classic pattern: a great new thing, prices that already discount a great future, and increasing amounts of leverage and new buyers coming in with borrowed money. That doesn't tell you the technology is fake — the railroads were real, the internet was real — but a lot of the capital gets destroyed anyway. And right now a very large share of the market's value and a meaningful share of the economy's growth is coming from a handful of companies doing this spending. So you've created a situation where if that spending slows, you have a downturn, and if it keeps going, you're probably overbuilding. Either path has a cost.

The second problem is the distribution. This technology raises productivity — I'm sure of that — but the gains go to the owners of the capital and to a relatively small number of highly skilled people, and the costs fall on people whose work gets replaced. That's happening at a moment when the wealth gap and the values gap are already as large as they've been since the 1930s, and when we have a debt problem that's going to require sacrifice. Put a big labor displacement on top of a population that's already angry and politically polarized, and you're adding fuel to a fire that's already burning.

And the third is the geopolitics. Whoever wins this wins military power, not just economic power, which means the United States and China can't afford to lose it. That makes it a race, and races between great powers at the end of a cycle are how you get conflict.

So it's a productivity miracle arriving at the worst possible moment in the cycle. That's the problem.

sonnet-5.5.text:
Well, let me separate two things: the technology and the investment dynamic. I believe AI is a real, transformative technology, like the internet or the railroads. But a transformative technology and a good investment at any price are not the same thing.

When something is truly revolutionary, a lot of money pours in. Prices go up, the people who bought make money, and that attracts more buyers, many of them borrowing to buy. That's the classic bubble pattern. The prices start to reflect not what the thing is worth, but how much leverage and enthusiasm is behind it. I look at it as a mechanical process, and I've seen it many times in history. It happened with the railroads in the 1800s, with the 1920s boom in new technologies, and with the dot-com era.

The question is where we are in that process. When I run my bubble indicators, I look at whether prices are high relative to traditional measures of value, whether they're discounting a lot of future success, whether there's a lot of new buying by new buyers, whether purchases are being financed with debt, and whether people are making optimistic bets that lack the cash flow to support them. On a number of those measures, we're in bubble territory, though not at the extreme of the dot-com peak.

The other problem is concentration. A handful of companies now account for a large share of the market's value and its earnings growth, so a lot of people are exposed to the same bet without realizing it. And the spending is enormous. To fund it, companies are going to have to raise a lot of money, which means selling a lot of debt and equity. That adds supply to a market that has to absorb it.

The most important point is what actually pops a bubble. It's usually not that the technology disappoints. It's a tightening of money and credit, or a need to sell assets to raise cash, that collides with the high prices. So when I watch this, I'm watching the technology, but I'm also watching the cost and availability of capital.

Many of the companies that win in the long run go through a shakeout first. Many investors in the early railroads lost most of their money, even though railroads changed the world. So the problem is not that AI is a fad. It's that the investment process can run far ahead of the reality, and the wrong people can get hurt.

haiku-5.5.text:
I wouldn't say the investment itself is the problem. AI is going to be enormously productive, and that's exactly why capital is pouring in. The problem is the dynamic around it. When something looks this transformative, money moves faster than anyone can sensibly judge what it's worth. A lot of capital chases a few winners, valuations get pushed well ahead of any earnings they might produce, and a lot of the spending gets misallocated. We've seen that pattern before, with railroads and with the internet.

The second problem is distribution. The gains tend to concentrate among the people who own the technology and the capital, while many of the people whose work gets disrupted don't share in them. When that gap widens, it creates political tension, and that tension can end up being a bigger problem than the technology.

So the question I'd ask isn't whether AI is good or bad. It's whether the cycle around it gets out of balance, with too much debt and speculation on one side and too little sharing of the benefits on the other. Those imbalances are what cause the trouble.

r001.rationale: The response describes capital rushing into AI and valuations running ahead of earnings, but it does not explain that competition pressures AI developers to make large investments despite uncertainty about the revenue they will generate.

astra-6.text:
Well, you have to separate two things: what the technology does and what people pay for it. AI can be enormously beneficial, raise productivity, change how we work—and still be a bad investment if the price already assumes extraordinary success.

When something exciting comes along, everybody wants to participate. Money pours in, prices rise, and those rising prices seem to validate the excitement. But ultimately, those investments have to produce earnings. Everybody can’t be the winner, and even the winners can be overpriced. If borrowing is involved, the disappointment can spread beyond the people who made the original investment.

Then there’s the question of who benefits. If you own the technology, you may become much wealthier. If the technology replaces what you do for a living, you may face a very different outcome. So you can have greater productivity overall alongside greater wealth inequality and social conflict.

That’s the challenge: a technological advance doesn’t automatically produce a good financial outcome or a broadly shared economic benefit. How it’s financed, what you pay, and how society adapts all matter.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, because something can be very good for productivity and still create problems in how the benefits are distributed. If I can replace somebody’s work with artificial intelligence, that may be very profitable for me. But what happens to that person’s income? And who owns the technology? You can increase the total wealth while also increasing the gap between people who have capital and people who depend on selling their labor. That has economic and political consequences.

Then there’s the investment side. People see a revolutionary technology and assume that investing in it at almost any price is going to be a good investment. But those are two different questions: Will this technology change the world? And will you earn an adequate return on the price you’re paying? You can be right about the first and wrong about the second.

So I’m looking at both things: whether the money going in will produce the profits people expect, and what happens to the people whose work becomes less valuable.
